label: Nodules and non-healing ulcers
q: Is this malignant, infective, or inflammatory?
lead: A lesion that has not healed in six weeks needs a diagnosis, not another dressing. Three groups account for nearly all of them: skin cancer, chronic infection, and neutrophilic or vasculitic ulceration. The mistake that costs most is debriding or grafting a pyoderma gangrenosum, which makes it larger.

stop.l: Rapidly enlarging ulcer with a violaceous undermined border and severe pain
stop.a: Pyoderma gangrenosum. Do not debride, do not graft — pathergy will enlarge it. Biopsy the edge to exclude infection and malignancy, then immunosuppress. Screen for inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis and hematologic disease.

stop.l: Ulcer with surrounding crepitus, dusky skin, and pain out of proportion
stop.a: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection. Immediate surgical exploration. Imaging must not delay it.

stop.l: Chronic ulcer in a longstanding scar, burn or sinus that has changed
stop.a: Marjolin ulcer — squamous cell carcinoma arising in chronic scarring. Biopsy generously from several sites.

stop.l: Non-healing lesion in an immunosuppressed patient
stop.a: Deep fungal, atypical mycobacterial or nocardial infection, and malignancy, all become more likely and more atypical. Biopsy for histology and send tissue for bacterial, mycobacterial and fungal culture in the same sitting.

stop.l: Painless indurated ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy and recent sexual exposure
stop.a: Primary syphilis. Dark-field or PCR and serology. Treat and trace contacts.

stop.l: A firm red or violaceous nodule enlarging rapidly over a few weeks
stop.a: Biopsy urgently to exclude Merkel cell carcinoma and other aggressive malignancies. Rapid nodular growth in an older or immunosuppressed adult is a red flag.

stop.l: Diabetic foot ulcer that probes to bone, or with spreading erythema, or a hot swollen foot
stop.a: Diabetic foot infection with probable osteomyelitis, or an acute Charcot foot. Refer to a multidisciplinary foot service the same day for imaging, deep tissue culture, vascular assessment and immediate offloading. Do not send the person away weight-bearing on a dressing - limb loss follows delay, and the absence of pain means nothing here.

dx.look: A rapidly growing, firm, painless, red to violaceous dome-shaped nodule on sun-exposed skin of an older or immunosuppressed adult, with a shiny intact surface; it grows over weeks and metastasizes early. The AEIOU features - Asymptomatic, Expanding rapidly, Immunosuppressed, Older than 50, UV-exposed - are a useful prompt.
fr: Rapidly enlarging over weeks
Firm, painless, red-violaceous shiny nodule
Sun-exposed head, neck or limb
Older than 50 or immunosuppressed
No overlying scale or ulceration early
ag: A central keratotic plug or a pearly rolled telangiectatic border (BCC or SCC)
dx.cf: Urgent biopsy - histology shows a small round blue-cell tumor, and CK20 in a perinuclear dot pattern with TTF-1 negativity confirms it; refer for sentinel-node biopsy and staging without delay.
dx.dsc: Nonspecific - a red-pink nodule with milky-red areas and linear irregular vessels; dermoscopy cannot exclude it, so biopsy any rapidly growing nodule.
dx.hp: A dermal small round blue-cell tumor with scant cytoplasm, smudged chromatin and brisk mitoses; CK20 stains in a perinuclear dot pattern and TTF-1 is negative (separating it from small-cell lung cancer).
dx.assoc: Merkel cell polyomavirus and immunosuppression are key drivers, and it metastasizes early, so sentinel-node biopsy and staging are essential; recurrence and nodal disease are common.
dx.mgmt: Wide local excision (or Mohs) with sentinel-node biopsy and usually adjuvant radiotherapy; immune-checkpoint inhibitors (avelumab, pembrolizumab) for advanced disease. Refer urgently.

dx.look: Crops of tender, red, warm, ill-defined subcutaneous nodules on the shins (rarely ulcerating) that evolve through bruise-like color changes and resolve without scarring over weeks; the commonest septal panniculitis and a reactive marker of an underlying trigger.
fr: Tender, bruise-like, non-ulcerating nodules on the anterior shins
Bilateral and symmetric
Resolution without scarring over 3 to 6 weeks
Fever, arthralgia and malaise
A recent infection, drug or new diagnosis (sarcoid, IBD)
ag: A purely epidermal or scaly lesion
dx.cf: A clinical diagnosis - search for the trigger (streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, drugs, pregnancy, and regionally TB or deep fungal infection) with a throat swab or ASO, chest imaging and a drug review.
dx.hp: A septal panniculitis - widened fibrous septa with a mixed infiltrate and Miescher radial granulomas - without vasculitis; a deep incisional biopsy including fat is needed if biopsied.
dx.assoc: A reactive marker - search for streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, drugs (OCPs, sulfonamides) and pregnancy; regionally, tuberculosis and deep fungal infection.
dx.mgmt: Treat the underlying cause; rest, leg elevation and NSAIDs, with potassium iodide or colchicine for persistent disease. Most resolve spontaneously.

dx.look: Pearly translucent papule or nodule with a rolled border and arborizing telangiectasia, often with central ulceration — the rodent ulcer. Slow growth over months to years. Head and neck, chronically sun-exposed. Rarely metastasizes but destroys locally.
fr: Pearly translucency with a rolled border
Arborizing telangiectasia over the surface
Slow growth over months to years
Chronically sun-exposed site, head and neck
Bleeds with minor trauma and scabs repeatedly
dx.cf: Punch or shave biopsy. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels, leaf-like areas and blue-gray ovoid nests with no pigment network.
dx.dsc: Arborizing vessels, blue-gray ovoid nests and leaf-like areas, spoke-wheel structures and ulceration, without a pigment network.
dx.hp: Basaloid nests with peripheral palisading, retraction clefts and a fibromyxoid stroma; the nodular type is low-risk, while morpheaform, infiltrative and micronodular types are high-risk.
dx.assoc: Cumulative UV on the head and neck; multiple or young-onset lesions raise basal cell nevus syndrome or prior radiation. Once one occurs, recurrence risk is high.
dx.mgmt: Surgical excision, with Mohs for high-risk or facial sites; topical or superficial options (imiquimod, curettage) for low-risk superficial lesions; hedgehog inhibitors for advanced disease.

dx.look: Firm, indurated, hyperkeratotic or ulcerated nodule with an everted or rolled edge on sun-damaged skin, often arising in an actinic keratosis. Tender. Grows over weeks to months. Metastatic potential, particularly on lip, ear, and in immunosuppressed patients.
fr: Firm, indurated base you can feel beyond the visible edge
Hyperkeratotic or ulcerated with an everted edge
Tender
Background actinic damage or a scar or chronic sinus
Immunosuppression or organ transplant
ag: Pearly translucency with fine arborizing vessels
dx.cf: Incisional or excisional biopsy including the deep edge. Assess for perineural symptoms and regional nodes — both change staging and management.
dx.dsc: A central keratin mass with hairpin and glomerular (coiled) vessels, white circles around follicles, and scale - a keratinizing pattern.
dx.hp: Atypical keratinocytes invading the dermis with keratin pearls; differentiation, depth and perineural invasion drive the risk.
dx.assoc: Sun-exposed sites, immunosuppression (transplant recipients), chronic wounds or scars (Marjolin ulcer), and HPV. Higher metastatic risk than BCC - assess the nodes.
dx.mgmt: Surgical excision (Mohs for high-risk sites); radiation for non-surgical candidates; nodal evaluation and systemic therapy for advanced or metastatic disease.

dx.look: Weeks to months after a sandfly bite on an exposed site: a papule enlarging to a nodule and then to a shallow ulcer with a raised indurated rolled border and an adherent crust. Painless. Satellite papules and nodular lymphangitis. Indolent over months.
fr: Residence in or travel to an endemic area
Exposed site — face, forearm, lower leg
Painless and indolent over months
Raised indurated rolled border with adherent crust
Satellite papules or a sporotrichoid chain
dx.cf: Slit-skin smear from the indurated edge with Giemsa staining for amastigotes, plus PCR for speciation, which determines whether systemic therapy is needed. Culture on NNN medium where available.
dx.dsc: Yellow tears and central erosion with peripheral hairpin or comma vessels and white starburst-like structures over an erythematous background.
dx.hp: A granulomatous dermal infiltrate with amastigotes inside macrophages (the marquee sign).
dx.assoc: Travel or residence in an endemic area with a chronic non-healing nodule or ulcer; confirm by smear, PCR (which speciates), or culture. Consider mucosal risk with New-World species.
dx.mgmt: Local therapy (cryotherapy, intralesional antimony, thermotherapy) for simple Old-World lesions; systemic antimonials, liposomal amphotericin B or miltefosine for complex or mucosal disease.

dx.look: Begins as a tender pustule or nodule that breaks down rapidly into an ulcer with a violaceous, undermined, overhanging border and a boggy necrotic base. Severe pain. Pathergy — it enlarges after trauma or surgery. Lower legs most often. Heals with a cribriform scar.
fr: Violaceous undermined overhanging border
Pain out of proportion to size
Rapid enlargement over days
Pathergy — worsened by debridement, biopsy or surgery
Inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritis, or a hematologic disorder
Cribriform scarring at healed sites
dx.cf: A diagnosis of exclusion. Biopsy the edge — mainly to exclude infection, vasculitis and malignancy — and send tissue for bacterial, mycobacterial and fungal culture. Then screen for the systemic associations. Do not debride.
dx.hp: A diagnosis of exclusion - early lesions show a suppurative folliculitis and a dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate; biopsy chiefly excludes infection, vasculitis and occlusion.
dx.assoc: Around half of patients have an associated disease - inflammatory bowel disease (most common), inflammatory arthritis, and hematologic disease or IgA gammopathy; pathergy is characteristic. Screen with CBC, SPEP and colonoscopy as indicated.
dx.mgmt: Systemic corticosteroids (about 1 mg/kg/day) first-line; cyclosporine or infliximab for aggressive or refractory disease; gentle wound care and avoid aggressive debridement (pathergy).

dx.look: A dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin-filled crater, growing rapidly over 4–8 weeks, then stabilizing and often involuting over months. Sun-exposed skin. Histologically and behaviorally overlaps with well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.
fr: Rapid growth over 4–8 weeks then a plateau
Symmetric dome with a central keratin plug
Sun-exposed site
Well-defined shoulders around the crater
ag: Asymmetric with an irregular infiltrating base
dx.cf: Excise it. Do not observe for involution: keratoacanthoma cannot be reliably distinguished from well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma without a full-thickness specimen showing the architecture, and a partial biopsy will not do it.
dx.dsc: A central keratin plug with peripheral hairpin and looped vessels and white halos - overlapping with well-differentiated SCC.
dx.hp: A crateriform, symmetric squamoproliferative lesion with a keratin-filled center and glassy keratinocytes; regarded as a well-differentiated variant of SCC.
dx.assoc: Rapid growth over weeks with possible involution; multiple lesions suggest Muir-Torre syndrome or prior immunosuppression. Treat as SCC given the overlap.
dx.mgmt: Surgical excision is preferred (do not rely on spontaneous regression); intralesional methotrexate or 5-fluorouracil for selected cases.

dx.n: Atypical mycobacterial or deep fungal infection
dx.look: Indolent nodules, plaques or ulcers, sometimes in a sporotrichoid chain along lymphatics. Follows aquarium or water exposure (Mycobacterium marinum), gardening or plant trauma (sporotrichosis), or surgery and cosmetic procedures (rapidly growing mycobacteria). Culture-negative on routine media — which is why it is missed.
fr: Indolent over weeks to months
Linear sporotrichoid chain of nodules along a lymphatic
Aquarium, water, soil or plant exposure
Recent surgical or cosmetic procedure
Routine bacterial cultures repeatedly negative
No response to standard antibiotics
ag: Prompt response to a standard antibiotic
dx.cf: Tissue for histology plus mycobacterial and fungal culture — you must ask for these specifically. Tell the laboratory to hold mycobacterial cultures at 30–32 °C as well as 37 °C, or Mycobacterium marinum will not grow.
dx.hp: Suppurative and granulomatous dermal inflammation; special stains (acid-fast, PAS or GMS) and, critically, tissue culture make the diagnosis.
dx.assoc: A chronic nodule or ulcer after aquatic or gardening exposure, or in immunosuppression (M. marinum, sporotrichosis, others); send fresh tissue for mycobacterial and fungal culture, not just histology.
dx.mgmt: Pathogen-specific and prolonged - for example clarithromycin-based regimens for M. marinum, or itraconazole for sporotrichosis; treat per culture and sensitivities.

dx.look: Venous: shallow, irregular, exudative ulcer over the medial malleolus, with hemosiderin pigmentation, varicosities, lipodermatosclerosis and edema. Arterial: punched-out, painful, dry, on the toes, heel or pretibial shin, with absent pulses, cool skin and hair loss.
fr: Venous: medial malleolus, shallow, exudative, with brown pigmentation and edema
Arterial: punched-out, dry, on toes or heel, with absent pulses and rest pain
Longstanding venous disease or peripheral arterial disease
Improves with elevation (venous) or worsens with it (arterial)
ag: Violaceous undermined border with disproportionate pain
dx.cf: Ankle-brachial pressure index before any compression. Biopsy any leg ulcer that has failed to heal after 3 months of appropriate treatment — malignancy hides in chronic ulcers.
dx.hp: Not usually biopsied; sample the ulcer rim only when a neoplasm or vasculitis is suspected in a non-healing ulcer.
dx.assoc: Venous (medial malleolus, hemosiderin, edema) versus arterial (distal, punched-out, painful, absent pulses) - check the ankle-brachial pressure index before any compression.
dx.mgmt: Venous - compression therapy after excluding arterial disease, with wound care; arterial - vascular referral for revascularization. Biopsy chronic non-healing ulcers to exclude malignancy.

dx.look: A mobile, dome-shaped, skin-colored dermal nodule with a central punctum, present for months to years, that becomes suddenly red, hot, painful and fluctuant when it ruptures. The inflammation is a foreign-body reaction to keratin, not usually infection.
fr: Long-standing painless nodule before the acute episode
Central punctum
Mobile over deep tissue
Foul-smelling cheesy keratin when it discharges
ag: Progressive growth without an inflammatory episode
dx.cf: Clinical. Incision and drainage relieves the acute episode, but the cyst wall must be excised once quiet or it recurs. Culture if there is surrounding cellulitis.
dx.dsc: A central punctum with a surrounding structureless whitish-yellow area; not a vascular pattern.
dx.hp: A cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with a granular layer and filled with laminated keratin; rupture provokes a foreign-body granulomatous reaction.
dx.assoc: A ruptured cyst inflames and mimics an abscess but is usually sterile; multiple cysts at unusual sites suggest Gardner syndrome.
dx.mgmt: For an acutely inflamed cyst, incision and drainage or an intralesional corticosteroid; excise the whole cyst wall once quiet to prevent recurrence.

dx.look: A hot, red, exquisitely tender nodule that becomes fluctuant over days, often with a central pustule or necrotic plug and a surrounding zone of cellulitis. A carbuncle is several coalescing furuncles with sieve-like openings draining pus. Any hair-bearing region - beard, posterior neck, axillae, buttocks - or any site of trauma.
fr: Evolves over days rather than weeks or months
Hot, red and exquisitely tender
Fluctuant, with a central pustule or necrotic plug
Surrounding cellulitis
Discharges frank pus and improves promptly after drainage
Diabetes, nasal Staphylococcus aureus carriage or recurrent boils
ag: No fluctuance and no pus at any stage
dx.cf: Clinical. Incise and drain, and send the pus for culture and sensitivities - MRSA is common and changes the antibiotic. Two traps are worth naming: a recurrent abscess at the same flexural site is hidradenitis suppurativa, and a recurrent abscess at the same non-flexural site is usually a ruptured epidermoid cyst whose wall has never been removed.
dx.hp: A dermal and subcutaneous collection of neutrophils with tissue necrosis centered on a hair follicle, walled by granulation tissue; gram-positive cocci on Gram stain.
dx.assoc: Staphylococcus aureus, increasingly MRSA. Recurrent furunculosis warrants screening for diabetes, nasal and household carriage, and rarely immunodeficiency; obesity and close contact sports are risk factors.
dx.mgmt: Incision and drainage is the treatment. Add an antistaphylococcal antibiotic with MRSA cover when there is cellulitis, systemic upset, immunosuppression, or a facial or large lesion. Decolonize with intranasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine washes for recurrent disease.

dx.look: Recurrent, exquisitely tender deep red nodules and abscesses in apocrine-bearing skin - axillae, groin, inframammary and anogenital - with double or paired open comedones, draining sinus tracts, and rope-like bridged scars. Pressure over a sinus expresses malodorous purulent exudate. Bilateral, and recurring in the same sites for years.
fr: Axillae, groin, inframammary or anogenital sites
Double or paired open comedones
Recurrent tender nodules and abscesses in the same sites
Draining sinus tracts and bridged rope-like scars
Obesity, smoking or a family history
Bilateral involvement
ag: A single lesion at a non-flexural site
dx.cf: A clinical diagnosis from the site, the recurrence and the paired comedones; no test confirms it and none is needed. Culture only guides antibiotics in a secondarily infected lesion, and ultrasound or MRI maps sinus tracts before surgery. Any longstanding perianal or gluteal sinus that changes needs biopsy for squamous cell carcinoma.
dx.hp: Keratin occlusion and dilatation of the follicular infundibulum with rupture, a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate confined to the follicular apparatus, destruction of the apocrine and pilosebaceous apparatus, fibrosis, and epithelialized sinus tracts with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia.
dx.assoc: Obesity, smoking and family history are the main drivers. Screen for metabolic syndrome, depression and inflammatory bowel disease. Severe disease causes anemia and, rarely, amyloidosis; longstanding anogenital disease carries a squamous cell carcinoma risk.
dx.mgmt: Weight loss and smoking cessation. Intralesional triamcinolone with incision and drainage for an acute painful nodule; clindamycin with rifampin, or a tetracycline, for chronic low-grade disease; adalimumab for moderate to severe disease; wide excision of established sinus tracts. It is not simply an infection, and antibiotics alone will not control it.

dx.look: A punched-out ulcer at a plantar pressure point - the great toe, a metatarsal head or the heel - ringed by thick callus, in a warm foot with palpable pulses. It is painless, which is why it presents late and why it probes to bone. Clawed toes, an insensate foot and a Charcot midfoot are the setting.
fr: Plantar pressure point: great toe, metatarsal head or heel
Ring of callus surrounding a punched-out ulcer
Painless despite its depth
Absent protective sensation and absent ankle reflexes
Longstanding diabetes with a warm foot and palpable pulses
Foot deformity, clawed toes or Charcot changes
ag: Medial malleolar site with hemosiderin pigmentation and edema
dx.cf: Test with a 10 g monofilament and palpate the pulses, then probe the ulcer - a sterile probe that reaches bone means osteomyelitis until imaging says otherwise. Plain radiographs first and MRI when the answer changes management; take deep tissue for culture and never a surface swab.
dx.hp: Not usually biopsied. Sample the ulcer rim only when a neoplasm is suspected in a chronic non-healing ulcer, and bone biopsy when osteomyelitis must be proven.
dx.assoc: Sensory, motor and autonomic neuropathy of longstanding diabetes, frequently combined with peripheral arterial disease and infection. Osteomyelitis complicates a large minority of deep ulcers and drives amputation risk. Assess perfusion in every case, because a neuropathic ulcer and an ischemic one often coexist in the same foot.
dx.mgmt: Offloading is the treatment - total contact casting or a removable knee-high walker - with sharp debridement of callus and necrotic tissue, glycemic control, culture-directed antibiotics for infection, and vascular assessment with revascularization where perfusion is inadequate. Refer to a multidisciplinary foot service.

dx.look: A single, small, firm, well-defined dome-shaped nodule under 1 cm on the free border of the helix or antihelix, often white-waxy and translucent with a central crust or small ulcer and sloping margins. The defining feature is pain - stabbing, spontaneous or on pressure, and severe enough to wake the sufferer when that ear touches the pillow.
fr: Free border of the helix or antihelix
Exquisite tenderness on point pressure
Wakes the sleeper when that ear is lain on
Small, under 1 cm, and static in size
Central crust or small ulcer over a firm nodule
Older man with chronic photodamage
ag: Arborizing telangiectasia over a pearly translucent surface
dx.cf: The pressure-related pain and the site make the diagnosis, but it looks exactly like a basal or squamous cell carcinoma on a sun-damaged ear, so biopsy or excision is usually justified. Histology shows degenerate dermal collagen extruding through an ulcerated epidermis over damaged cartilage rather than tumor.
dx.dsc: A central yellowish structureless crust or ulcer surrounded by fine peripheral vessels over a white background. There are no arborizing vessels, no blue-gray ovoid nests and no keratin pearls - but dermoscopy alone should not be used to spare a biopsy on an older ear.
dx.hp: A central epidermal ulcer with a plug of degenerate, homogenized eosinophilic dermal collagen extruding through it, over vascular granulation tissue and degenerate or inflamed perichondrium and cartilage. No tumor.
dx.assoc: Chronic pressure and cumulative UV exposure, strongly associated with sleeping on that side. Bilateral disease or onset in a younger person should prompt a look for a connective tissue disease.
dx.mgmt: Pressure offloading with a foam ear pad or a prosthetic pillow cures many cases and should be tried first. Intralesional triamcinolone for persistent pain, and excision including the underlying cartilage as the definitive treatment.

dx.look: Violaceous to brown-black macules that thicken into oval plaques oriented along skin tension lines and then into confluent nodules, with disproportionate lymphedema of the affected limb. Classic disease favors the feet and legs of older men of Mediterranean or Ashkenazi descent; HIV-associated disease involves the face, trunk and hard palate early and progresses fast.
fr: Violaceous to brown-black color throughout
Multiple lesions progressing from macule to plaque to nodule
Oval plaques aligned along skin tension lines
Disproportionate lymphedema of the same limb
HIV infection, transplantation or other immunosuppression
Violaceous lesions on the hard palate
ag: A solitary pearly nodule with arborizing vessels
A purely keratotic surface with a central plug
No violaceous or pigmented hue at any stage
dx.cf: Biopsy with HHV-8 (LANA-1) immunostaining confirms it. Test for HIV in every case whatever the presumed variant, review any immunosuppressive drugs, and stage with oral examination, chest imaging and gastrointestinal assessment.
dx.dsc: A rainbow pattern of multicolored bands under polarized dermoscopy over a bluish-red homogeneous background, with scaly and whitish veils - highly suggestive but not a substitute for biopsy.
dx.hp: Proliferating spindle cells forming slit-like vascular channels with extravasated erythrocytes and hemosiderin, plasma cells at the periphery, and nuclear staining for HHV-8 latent nuclear antigen.
dx.assoc: Invariably linked to HHV-8. Four variants - classic, African endemic, iatrogenic after transplantation, and HIV/AIDS-associated. Visceral disease of the gut and lung is common and often asymptomatic; lymph nodes are involved in half of HIV-associated cases.
dx.mgmt: Restore immune function first - antiretroviral therapy for HIV-associated disease, and reduction of immunosuppression after transplantation, which alone often produces regression. Local therapy (radiotherapy, intralesional vinblastine, cryotherapy) for limited disease; liposomal anthracycline or paclitaxel for extensive or visceral disease.
dx.pat: Feet and legs, or face and palate

dx.look: One or several firm to stony-hard dermal or subcutaneous nodules with intact, stretched, skin-colored or pink-red epidermis over them, growing steadily over weeks. Scalp, chest wall, abdomen and surgical scars are the usual sites. Breast cancer also produces an erysipelas-like inflammatory plaque (carcinoma erysipelatoides) and a woody sclerodermoid plate (carcinoma en cuirasse); scalp deposits produce alopecia neoplastica.
fr: Firm to stony-hard dermal nodule with intact stretched skin over it
Several lesions appearing over a short period
Scalp, chest wall, abdomen, or in or beside a surgical scar
Known or suspected internal malignancy
Steady painless growth without ulceration early
An erysipelas-like or morphea-like plate on the chest wall
ag: A central punctum discharging cheesy keratin
dx.cf: Biopsy any new firm dermal nodule in someone with a cancer history. Histology plus an immunohistochemical panel (CK7, CK20, TTF-1, GATA3, CDX2 and others) identifies the organ of origin. Where there is no known primary, the skin lesion is the presenting sign of disseminated disease and drives a full staging work-up.
dx.hp: Nests, cords or single-file strands of atypical epithelial cells within the dermis and dermal lymphatics, with an uninvolved epidermis over a grenz zone; the architecture and immunophenotype indicate the primary.
dx.assoc: Most often breast in women and lung in men, then colorectal, renal, ovarian and melanoma. A Sister Mary Joseph nodule at the umbilicus signals intra-abdominal malignancy. The finding indicates disseminated disease and mandates oncology referral and staging.
dx.mgmt: Treat the underlying malignancy - the skin lesion is a marker of dissemination, not a local problem. Local measures (excision, radiotherapy, electrochemotherapy, topical miltefosine) for symptomatic, bleeding or malodorous deposits, and specialist wound care for fungating lesions.

ctx.l: Endemic area for leishmaniasis (Middle East, North Africa, Central Asia, Latin America)
ctx.s: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is endemic across the Arabian peninsula, Fitzpatrick 8e §29
Squamous cell carcinoma risk rises up to 65-fold after organ transplantation, Fitzpatrick 8e §11

ctx.l: Known inflammatory bowel disease or inflammatory arthritis
Aquarium, soil, plant or water exposure
Arose within an old scar, burn or chronic sinus

ctx.s: Chronicity shifts strongly toward neoplasia and chronic infection

ctx.l: HIV infection or other significant immunodeficiency
ctx.s: HIV raises Kaposi sarcoma risk by orders of magnitude, Fitzpatrick 8e §21

ctx.l: Known internal malignancy, current or previously treated
Obesity, smoking or a family history of hidradenitis

find.l: Pearly translucency with arborizing telangiectasia
Firm indurated base extending beyond the visible edge
Violaceous, undermined, overhanging ulcer border
Pain far out of proportion to the size of the lesion
Enlarged after debridement, biopsy or surgery (pathergy)
find.s: Pathergy is characteristic of pyoderma gangrenosum, Fitzpatrick 8e §15

find.l: Completely painless
Raised indurated rolled border with an adherent crust
Linear chain of nodules along a lymphatic (sporotrichoid)
Rapid growth over 4–8 weeks then plateau
Central keratin-filled crater with well-defined shoulders
Central punctum, mobile over deep tissue
Over the medial malleolus with brown pigmentation and edema
Absent peripheral pulses with a punched-out, dry, painful ulcer
No response to two or more courses of standard antibiotics
find.s: Antibiotic failure should trigger biopsy and culture for atypical organisms

find.l: Bleeds easily with minor trauma and scabs repeatedly
A firm red-violaceous nodule enlarging rapidly over weeks
Tender bruise-like non-ulcerating nodules on both shins
Recurrent tender nodules and draining sinuses in the axillae, groin or anogenital skin
Double or paired open comedones beside the lesion
find.s: Paired comedones are characteristic of hidradenitis suppurativa, Fitzpatrick 8e §1

find.l: Hot and fluctuant, evolving over days rather than weeks
Discharges frank pus and improves promptly after drainage
Violaceous to brown-black plaques aligned along skin tension lines
Multiple lesions with disproportionate lymphedema of the same limb
Several firm dermal nodules with intact stretched skin appearing over weeks
Small nodule on the free border of the ear that wakes the sleeper when lain on
Punched-out plantar ulcer at a pressure point ringed by callus
Absent protective sensation to a 10 g monofilament in a warm foot with palpable pulses
Fever, malaise and ankle arthralgia accompanying the leg nodules
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §7 - fever, malaise and arthralgia of the ankles accompany about half of erythema nodosum

test.l: Biopsy with CK20 and TTF-1 immunostaining
test.w: Any rapidly growing firm red-violaceous nodule in an older or immunosuppressed adult.
test.p: A small round blue-cell tumor with CK20 in a perinuclear dot pattern and negative TTF-1 confirms Merkel cell carcinoma. Refer for sentinel-node biopsy and staging urgently.
test.n: A negative result redirects to other small round-cell tumors - correlate with CK7 and TTF-1 to exclude metastatic small-cell carcinoma.
test.x: Do not delay - Merkel cell carcinoma metastasizes early; refer at the same time as biopsy if suspicion is high.

test.l: Incisional biopsy including the deep edge
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction — all ulcers and inflammatory dermal nodules should be biopsied at base and margin
test.w: Any nodule or ulcer that has not healed in 6 weeks, and any lesion where malignancy is possible. Take a wedge that includes all three layers of skin.
test.p: Establishes the diagnosis and, for carcinoma, the depth, differentiation and perineural involvement that determine treatment.
test.n: A superficial or peripheral sample can miss the diagnostic tissue entirely. Depth matters more than width.
test.x: Split the specimen: half to histopathology in formalin, half minced fresh to microbiology for bacterial, mycobacterial and fungal culture. Taking only one half is the commonest reason a chronic ulcer stays undiagnosed after biopsy.

test.l: Tissue culture: bacterial, mycobacterial and fungal
test.w: Every chronic ulcer or nodule, in the same sitting as the biopsy. Surface swabs of a chronic ulcer report colonizers, not pathogens.
test.p: Identifies the organism and its sensitivities, which for atypical mycobacteria and deep fungi determines a treatment course lasting months.
test.n: Negative culture does not exclude atypical infection — yield is low and slow. Repeat, and consider PCR on tissue.
test.x: Tell the laboratory what you suspect. Mycobacterial cultures must be incubated at 30–32 °C as well as 37 °C or Mycobacterium marinum will not grow, and standard hold times are too short for slow growers.

test.l: Slit-skin smear with Giemsa, plus PCR for speciation
test.w: Any chronic painless ulcerated nodule with a raised border in a patient from or returning from an endemic area. In endemic practice, this should be an early test rather than a late one.
test.p: Amastigotes within macrophages confirm it. Speciation determines management: some species carry mucosal risk and require systemic treatment rather than local therapy.
test.n: Sensitivity falls as the lesion ages and parasites become scanty. A negative smear with a compatible history warrants PCR or biopsy.
test.x: Sample the indurated edge after cleaning and de-crusting, not the ulcer floor. The floor yields necrotic debris and contaminating bacteria and is the usual reason for a false negative.

test.l: Biopsy of the ulcer edge, with screening for systemic associations
test.w: A rapidly enlarging, severely painful ulcer with an undermined violaceous border. The biopsy exists to exclude the alternatives, since pyoderma gangrenosum has no positive histologic marker.
test.p: A dense neutrophilic infiltrate with no organisms, no vasculitis and no malignancy, in the right clinical setting, supports it. Then screen for inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritis, and hematologic disease including monoclonal gammopathy.
test.n: Finding an organism, a vasculitis or a tumor rules it out and gives you the real diagnosis instead.
test.x: This is the one place where biopsy carries a therapeutic risk: pathergy can enlarge the ulcer. Take a small elliptical sample from the edge, and never let anyone debride or graft this ulcer while the diagnosis is open.

test.w: Every leg ulcer, before any compression bandage is applied.
test.p: Above 0.8 permits full compression, which is the treatment for venous ulceration. Below 0.5 indicates critical ischemia and needs urgent vascular referral.
test.n: A normal index confirms compression is safe and directs treatment toward venous management.
test.x: Falsely elevated in diabetes and chronic kidney disease because of medial calcification. Use toe pressures or waveform analysis in those patients. Applying compression to an ischemic leg causes tissue loss.

test.l: Incision and drainage, with pus sent for culture and sensitivities
test.w: Any hot, fluctuant, tender nodule that has evolved over days. Do not wait for antibiotics to work on a collection - drainage is the treatment, and the specimen is a by-product of it.
test.p: Frank pus with Staphylococcus aureus on culture confirms it and gives the sensitivities. MRSA is common enough that empiric cover should assume it until the result returns, and recurrence should trigger nasal and household decolonization.
test.n: No pus at incision means this was not an abscess. Reconsider a ruptured cyst, hidradenitis, an inflamed tumor or pyoderma gangrenosum, and send tissue rather than a swab.
test.x: The error that matters is repeated drainage of the same site without asking why. A third abscess in the same axilla or groin is hidradenitis suppurativa, and a third at the same non-flexural site is a cyst wall that was never excised. Neither is cured by another course of flucloxacillin.

test.l: Biopsy with HHV-8 (LANA-1) immunostaining, plus HIV testing
test.w: Any violaceous or brown-black plaque or nodule, particularly when there are several, when they align along tension lines, or when a limb is disproportionately edematous.
test.p: Spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated erythrocytes and nuclear HHV-8 staining confirms Kaposi sarcoma. Then stage: examine the palate, image the chest, and assess the gut. Restoring immune function is the first therapeutic move.
test.n: A negative result redirects to the other violaceous mimics - bacillary angiomatosis, angiosarcoma, pyogenic granuloma, stasis change and pigmented purpura - several of which have entirely different treatment.
test.x: Two omissions recur. HIV testing gets skipped when the presentation looks like classic Mediterranean disease, and immunosuppressive drugs go unreviewed in transplant recipients. Both change management more than any local therapy does.

test.l: Biopsy with an immunohistochemical panel to identify the primary
test.w: Any new firm dermal or subcutaneous nodule in someone with a current or previous internal malignancy, and any cluster of firm nodules on the scalp or chest wall appearing over weeks.
test.p: Atypical epithelial cells in the dermis and dermal lymphatics under an uninvolved epidermis confirms metastasis, and the marker panel points to the organ of origin. Refer to oncology for staging - this changes the treatment intent, not just the wound plan.
test.n: A benign result in a compatible clinical picture warrants a second, deeper sample. Superficial biopsies of a subcutaneous deposit return dermal fibrosis and nothing else.
test.x: The commonest miss is the scalp nodule found after chemotherapy alopecia, dismissed as a cyst or folliculitis. Also remember carcinoma en cuirasse, which is a firm plate rather than a nodule and gets treated for months as morphea or cellulitis.

test.l: Probe-to-bone test with plain radiographs and deep tissue culture
test.w: Every diabetic foot ulcer at the first visit, alongside a 10 g monofilament test and pulse palpation. Debride the callus first, then probe gently with a sterile blunt probe.
test.p: A probe that reaches gritty bone makes osteomyelitis likely and mandates imaging, deep tissue culture and specialist referral. Deep tissue or bone culture directs antibiotics, which will run for weeks.
test.n: A negative probe does not exclude osteomyelitis, particularly early, and plain films lag the infection by two weeks or more. Repeat the film or move to MRI if the ulcer fails to progress.
test.x: The two habitual errors are swabbing the ulcer surface, which grows colonizers and drives futile antibiotic courses, and applying compression or leaving the person weight-bearing. Offloading heals these ulcers; dressings do not. Check perfusion before assuming the ulcer is purely neuropathic.

test.l: Trial of pressure offloading with a foam ear pad
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin; calibrated estimate
test.w: A small, painful nodule on the helix or antihelix where the history is of pressure-related pain and there is no clinical suspicion of carcinoma.
test.p: Substantial improvement in pain over 4 to 8 weeks of consistent offloading supports chondrodermatitis and can spare surgery. Intralesional triamcinolone is the next step if pain persists.
test.n: Failure to improve, or any growth, ulceration or induration, means biopsy. A painless or enlarging nodule on a sun-damaged ear is a carcinoma until histology says otherwise.
test.x: Do not use the trial as a reason to defer biopsy in an older person with marked photodamage. Basal and squamous cell carcinoma of the ear present exactly this way, and the ear is a high-risk site where delay costs cartilage.

flag: Any ulcer that has not healed after three months of appropriate treatment must be biopsied, whatever the presumed cause. Squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic venous ulcer is found late precisely because everyone assumed they already knew what it was.
